ai_analysis.title_ko: 군위 지역 신동그룹 사암의 속성작용 및 속성 광물상
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 군위 지역 신동그룹 사암에서 발견되는 자생 광물은 탄산염 광물(방해석, 능철석, 돌로마이트), 점토 광물(일라이트, 녹니석, 일라이트-스멕타이트 혼합층, 녹니석-스멕타이트 혼합층), 석영, 장석(알바이트 및 칼륨장석), 그리고 적철석이다. 이들은 각 층군에서 특징적인 속성 광물상을 형성한다. 즉 낙동층은 일라이트+석영, 하사동층은 일라이트+방해석+알바이트, 진주층은 일라이트+방해석+녹니석+알바이트 조합을 보인다. 사암의 주요 자생 시멘트 물질인 방해석은 주로 매몰 속성작용 동안 올리고클래스 조성을 가진 사장석 쇄설물의 알바이트화 작용의 결과로 부분적으로 형성되었다. 사장석의 알바이트화는 평균 약 70% 정도 진행되었다. 이와 더불어 스멕타이트계 점토 광물이 일라이트나 녹니석으로 전이되는 과정도 사암의 방해석 시멘트 형성에 칼슘 공급원으로 중요한 역할을 했다. 사암과 셰일의 교호대에서는 사장석의 알바이트화보다는 점토질 속성 변화가 사암 내 방해석 형성을 조절하는 주요 요인으로 작용하는 것으로 나타났다. 일라이트 다형성에 대한 X선 회절 분석을 바탕으로, 신동그룹의 퇴적물은 약 200~250℃ 범위의 매몰 속성작용을 겪은 것으로 추정된다. 백악기 화강암의 관입이 퇴적물에 미친 온도 영향은 미미하고 무시할 수 있는 수준으로 보인다. 이 온도 범위는 팔공산 화강암 남서쪽에 위치한 고령 지역의 경우보다 지층의 매몰 깊이가 더 깊었음을 반영할 수 있다. 고령 지역에 비해 더 높은 알바이트화 진행 도와 우세한 일라이트 결정화도는 이러한 가정을 뒷받침한다.
summary_3lines: 군위 지역 신동그룹 사암의 자생 광물 분포와 속성작용 특성을 분석하여 지질학적 매몰 환경을 규명하고자 하였다.
X선 회절 분석 등을 통해 사암 내 탄산염 및 점토 광물의 상 변화와 사장석의 알바이트화 과정을 정밀 분석하였다.
연구 결과 신동그룹 퇴적물은 약 200~250℃의 매몰 속성작용을 거쳤으며, 화강암 관입의 영향은 적고 깊은 매몰 깊이를 반영함을 확인하였다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구는 경북 군위 지역에 분포하는 신동그룹 사암층의 자생 광물 조합과 속성작용 특성을 파악하고, 매몰 속성 과정에서 일어난 광물 상 변화와 온도 조건을 규명하는 것을 목적으로 한다. 이를 통해 지질학적 변천사와 광물 생성 원인을 밝히고자 하였다.
key_findings: 각 지층별로 낙동층(일라이트+석영), 하사동층(일라이트+방해석+알바이트), 진주층(일라이트+방해석+녹니석+알바이트)의 특징적인 속성 광물상을 확인함.
사암 내 방해석 시멘트는 사장석의 알바이트화 및 스멕타이트계 점토 광물의 전이에 따른 칼슘 공급으로 형성됨.
신동그룹 퇴적물은 약 200~250℃ 범위의 매몰 속성작용을 겪었으며 백악기 화강암 관입의 영향은 미미함.
practical_applications: 국립공원 내 지질유산 및 퇴적암 지형 조사 시 지층의 속성 환경과 광물 특성 분석 기초 자료로 활용
지질 탐방로 및 교육 프로그램 운영 시 공원 내 퇴적암의 생성 과정에 대한 학술적 설명 자료로 적용
지질학적 보존 가치가 높은 퇴적층의 안전성 및 풍화 특성 평가 시 광물 조성 분석 방법론 활용
ai_analysis.korea_np_applicability_reason: 본 논문은 특정 지역의 지질학적 속성작용과 광물 분석을 다룬 순수 기초과학 연구로, 일반적인 국립공원 탐방객 관리나 생태계 관리보다는 지질공원 운영 및 지질 자원 조사 분야에 국한되어 직접적인 현장 적용성은 상대적으로 낮음.
field_checklist: 국립공원 내 퇴적암 지역의 암상 및 층서별 자생 광물 분포 현황 확인
사암 및 셰일 교호대의 풍화 및 지질 변성 상태 점검
지질 명소 주변 암석의 탄산염 시멘트 및 점토 광물 조성 변화 모니터링
과거 매몰 온도 및 지열에 따른 지질 자원의 안정성 평가
인근 화강암 관입부와 퇴적암 경계부의 지질학적 특이사항 기록
cautions: 본 연구는 순수 지질학적 암석 분석에 초점을 맞추고 있어 직접적인 공원 관리 현장 적용에는 한계가 있음
시료 채취 및 분석 시 공원 내 자연자원 훼손 방지를 관련 법규에 따라 엄격히 관리해야 함
recommended_followup_research: 한반도 경상계 지층 전반에 걸친 속성 광물상 비교 연구
지질 유산의 풍화 메커니즘과 광물 조성 변화 간의 상관관계 분석

papers.title: Border Patrol: Questioning the Citizen in Citizen Scientist
papers.abstract: Border Patrol: Questioning the Citizen in Citizen Scientist Kevin A. Nguyen I stirred in my sleep and rolled over to my back. I opened my eyes and saw bright, beautiful, dancing stars framed by the two walls of Santa Elena Canyon. I was sleeping so hard that I forgot where I was and what I was doing. Cozied up in my sleeping bag, I had dreamt that I was back home dozing off in my warm apartment. Instead, I was outside in the cold air, laying on the grass of Camp Gourmet in December 2015. The nearby Rio Grande rushed past the camp, and its swirling current was loud enough to lull you back asleep. I checked my watch—3 am. I’d have to get up in four hours to help start making breakfast for the team and breaking down camp. Thinking about all I had to do kept me awake. I then thought about how it was the second night of our three-day trip into Santa Elena Canyon. In the morning, we’d paddle out of the canyon and leave the Rio Grande. We’d load the canoes onto the trailer and drive out of Big Bend National Park towards Alpine, Texas. It was two hours away and was the nearest and largest city for miles. Well, large, if you consider a town of about 6000 people large. The thought of driving to Alpine made me worry. We’d be coming from the Rio Grande, the political boundary between the United States and Mexico. Driving from this direction meant we’d have to go through Border Patrol and be stopped and potentially searched. When people think of a political boundary, they think of a fence, a gate, or even a wall. But none of these things exist along the Rio Grande. There is no sign that says, ‘Welcome to the United States!’ or ‘Bienvenidos a México!’ on the other side. Instead, the barren and remoteness of the area serve as its own boundary and the United States Border Patrol knows this. They wait at a checkpoint a few miles outside Alpine on the main road. They know that since there isn’t potable water for miles, immigrants making the trip to the US would most likely drive to Alpine to refuel and stock up. Tired of thinking about all of this, I turned [End Page 27] over and closed my eyes. I figured I shouldn’t have to worry. I mean, borders are an abstraction. They’re made up. Social constructs. Abstract like a dream. A bad dream. I fell asleep. I woke up to my cell phone alarm buzzing in the bag beside me. 7 am. It was bright outside as the sun was up too, but with the canyon walls so high our camp remained in the shadows. It was still quite cold. I threw on a beanie, some gloves, rolled up my sleeping bag, and headed towards the camp kitchen. Friends were already boiling water for coffee and frying eggs. I looked over towards the river and saw two people carrying out the water quality sampling kits. Thinking that breakfast was taken care of, I walked towards the two team members to help ‘do science.’ We were here as citizen scientists to monitor the water quality in remote locations along the Rio Grande. There wasn’t a USGS (United States Geological Services) monitoring station for long stretches of the river, and we knew that certain stretches of the river were in impaired zones. In other words, the water quality here was suspect, as heavy contaminants, fish kills, and dumping could be causes of concern. If there were point source contamination, neither the United States nor Mexico would find out until the contaminant was picked up miles away at a monitoring station. We were here to fill in the gaps. I smiled as I approached the two fellow citizen scientists, and we said our good mornings. I was handed a water quality kit, and one of the members went to the river to collect a few samples of river water. I opened the kit and exposed the two probes: one was for recording dissolved...

ai_analysis.title_ko: 국경 순찰: 시민과학 속의 '시민'에 대한 고찰
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 국경 순찰: 시민과학 속의 '시민'에 대한 고찰 케빈 A. 누겐트 나는 잠에서 깨어나 등 뒤로 몸을 돌렸다. 눈을 뜨자 산 엘레나 협곡의 양쪽 벽이 액자처럼 둘러싼 밝고 아름다운 별들이 춤추는 모습이 보였다. 너무 깊게 잠들어 내가 어디에 있고 무엇을 하고 있었는지도 잊어버리고 있었다. 침낭 속에서 포근하게 잠들어 있던 나는, 마치 집에 있는 따뜻한 아파트에서 깜빡 졸고 있는 꿈을 꾸고 있었다. 하지만 현실은 2015년 12월, 추운 공기 속에서 캠 그루메트의 잔디밭에 누워 있는 것이었다. 근처를 흐르는 리오그란데강은 캠프장을 스쳐 지나갔고, 그 소용돌이치는 물살은 다시 잠에 빠져들게 할 만큼 충분히 시끄러웠다. 시계를 보니 새벽 3시였다. 4시간 뒤에 일어나 팀의 아침 식사 준비를 돕고 캠프를 철수해야 했다. 해야 할 일들을 생각하니 잠이 깨어버렸다. 그리고 그때가 산 엘레나 협곡으로 떠난 3일간의 여정 중 둘째 날 밤이라는 생각이 스쳤다. 아침이면 우리는 협곡을 카누로 빠져나와 리오그란데강을 떠날 것이다. 우리는 카누를 트레일러에 싣고 빅벤드 국립공원을 빠져나와 텍사스주 알파인으로 향할 것이다. 그곳은 차로 2시간 거리에 있으며, 몇 마일 반경 내에서 가장 가깝고 가장 큰 도시였다. 물론 인구 6,000명 정도의 마을을 크다고 생각한다면 말이다. 알파인으로 운전해 갈 생각을 하니 걱정이 되었다. 우리는 미국과 멕시코 사이의 정치적 경계인 리오그란데강에서 출발하는 것이었다. 이 방향에서 운전해 간다는 것은 국경 순찰대를 거쳐 검문을 받고 잠재적으로 수색을 받을 수 있음을 의미했다. 사람들이 정치적 경계를 생각할 때, 그들은 울타리, 문, 혹은 심지어 벽을 떠올린다. 하지만 리오그란데강을 따라서는 이러한 것들이 전혀 존재하지 않는다. 반대편에 '미국에 오신 것을 환영합니다!'라거나 '멕시코에 오신 것을 환영합니다!'라고 쓰인 표지판도 없다. 대신, 그 지역의 황폐함과 오지라는 특성이 그 자체로 경계의 역할을 하며, 미국 국경 순찰대도 이를 잘 알고 있다. 그들은 알파인 외곽 몇 마일 떨어진 메인 도로의 검문소에서 기다린다. 그들은 수 마일 동안 마실 물이 없기 때문에 미국으로 향하는 이주민들이 연료를 채우고 보급품을 챙기기 위해 알파인으로 차를 몰고 갈 가능성이 높다는 것을 알고 있다. 이 모든 생각에 지쳐, 나는 몸을 돌려 눈을 감았다. 걱정할 필요가 없다고 생각했다. 즉, 국경은 추상적인 개념이기 때문이다. 그것들은 만들어진 것이다. 사회적 구성물이다. 꿈처럼 추상적이다. 악몽 같은 꿈. 나는 다시 잠들었다. 가방 옆에서 진동하는 휴대전화 알람 소리에 눈을 떴다. 아침 7시. 해가 떠서 밖은 밝았지만 협곡의 벽이 워낙 높아 우리 캠프장은 여전히 그늘에 잠겨 있었다. 날씨는 여전히 꽤 추웠다. 나는 비니를 쓰고, 장갑을 끼고, 침낭을 둘러멘 뒤 캠프 주방으로 향했다. 동료들은 이미 커피를 위한 물을 끓이고 달걀을 튀기고 있었다. 나는 강 쪽을 바라보며 두 사람이 수질 시료 채취 키트를 들고 나오는 것을 보았다. 아침 식사는 해결되었다고 생각하고, 나는 '과학 활동'을 돕기 위해 두 팀원에게 다가갔다. 우리는 리오그란데강의 원격지에서 수질을 모니터링하기 위해 시민과학자 신분으로 이곳에 와 있었다.
summary_3lines: 미국 빅벤드 국립공원 내 리오그란데강에서 진행된 시민과학 수질 모니터링 활동을 통해 자연환경 속 지리적·정치적 경계의 의미를 탐구하고자 함.
원격지 탐방 및 현장 조사를 수행하는 과정에서 국경 지역이라는 특수한 지정학적 환경과 국경 순찰대의 통제로 인한 긴장감을 문학적 서사로 기록함.
국립공원 내 시민과학 프로그램 운영 시, 오지 탐방에 수반되는 지리적 위험 요소와 정치·사회적 맥락을 고려한 현장 안전 관리 체계 마련의 필요성을 시사함.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구는 미국 빅벤드 국립공원과 멕시코 국경 인근의 리오그란데강에서 수행된 시민과학 수질 모니터링 활동의 경험을 바탕으로, 자연 환경 속에서 개인이 체감하는 정치적·지리적 경계의 의미를 탐구하는 것을 목적으로 한다. 오지 탐방과 과학 조사 활동이 결합된 현장에서 발생하는 지정학적 긴장감과 '시민'으로서의 정체성을 자전적 서사를 통해 고찰하고자 한다.
key_findings: 리오그란데강과 같은 자연 지형물은 물리적 인프라(울타리 등)가 없더라도 황폐한 오지라는 환경적 특성 자체로 강력한 정치적 국경의 역할을 수행함.
국립공원 내 원격지에서 진행되는 시민과학 활동은 단순한 환경 조사를 넘어 국경 검문소 및 순찰대의 통제와 같은 정치·사회적 현실에 직면하게 됨.
탐방객 및 시민과학자들은 자연을 탐구하는 주체인 동시에 국가의 감시와 통제 대상이 되는 이중적 정체성을 경험함.
practical_applications: 국경 인근이나 접경 지역에 위치한 국립공원에서 시민과학 프로그램 운영 시, 사전 안전 교육에 지역 지정학적 특수성 및 검문 절차 안내를 포함할 것.
오지 탐방 및 수질 조사 등 야외 조사 프로그램 기획 시, 통신 및 접근이 제한된 환경에서의 비상 상황 대응 매뉴얼을 정비할 것.

papers.title: Assessing the sustainability and resilience of cacao-cased farming systems in Pili, Camarines Sur, the Philippines
papers.abstract: Camarines Sur, located in the Bicol Region of the Philippines, is considered one of the most climate-vulnerable provinces. Despite this, it is a model for a robust and proactive disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) program. The province features a diverse agroecological landscape, ranging from hilly and rolling terrains to plains surrounding Mt. Isarog National Park, which covers an area of 10.112 hectares with an elevation reaching 1.966 meters above sea level. Farming systems include monocropping, intensive multiple cropping, and agroforestry, with sugarcane and corn on downslopes, groundnuts and vegetables on lower slopes, and irrigated or rainfed rice fields. The integration of cacao (Theobroma cacao L.) is increasingly being explored as a means to enhance both the sustainability and resilience of these farming systems. This study aims to assess the sustainability and resilience of cacao cultivation at the farm level in Barangay Binanuanan, Pili, Camarines Sur. A qualitative research design was employed, utilizing semi-structured interviews with local government officials, focus group discussions with farmers, and a Strengths, Opportunities, and Challenges (SOC) analysis. Findings indicate that cacao farming contributes to economic sustainability, as most farmers benefit from diversified income sources, including off-farm employment and family financial support. Ecological sustainability is supported by cacao’s compatibility with existing farming practices. However, social resilience remains limited, as evidenced by the aging farming population and minimal youth engagement in agriculture. To strengthen overall system resilience, targeted interventions promoting youth participation and community engagement in cacao-based farming are recommended.
papers.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Sustainable Agriculture Food and Energy

ai_analysis.title_ko: 필리핀 카마리네스수르 필리 지역의 카카오 기반 농업 시스템의 지속 가능성 및 회복력 평가
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 필리핀 비콜 지역에 위치한 카마리네스수르는 기후 변화에 가장 취약한 주로 꼽히지만, 강력하고 사전 예방적인 재해 위험 경감 및 관리(DRRM) 프로그램의 모범 사례이기도 합니다. 이 주는 10,112헥타르의 면적과 해발 1,966미터에 달하는 이사로그산 국립공원을 둘러싼 평원부터 구릉 및 완경사 지대에 이르기까지 다양한 농업 생태 경관을 자랑합니다. 농업 시스템은 단작, 집약적 다모작, 혼농임업 등으로 구성되며, 하사면에는 사탕수수와 옥수수, 하부 경사면에는 땅콩과 채소, 그리고 관수 또는 천수답 논이 있습니다. 카카오(Theobroma cacao L.)의 도입은 이러한 농업 시스템의 지속 가능성과 회복력을 모두 향상시키는 수단으로 점점 더 연구되고 있습니다. 본 연구는 카마리네스수르 필리 비나누아난 바랑가이의 농가 수준에서 카카오 경작의 지속 가능성과 회복력을 평가하는 것을 목표로 합니다. 지방 정부 관료와의 반구조화된 인터뷰, 농민 초점집단 토의(FGD), 강점·기회·과제(SOC) 분석을 활용한 질적 연구 설계를 채택했습니다. 연구 결과, 카카오 농업은 대부분의 농민이 농외 소득 및 가족 재정 지원을 포함한 다양한 소득원의 혜택을 받기 때문에 경제적 지속 가능성에 기여하는 것으로 나타났습니다. 생태적 지속 가능성은 기존 농업 관행과 카카오의 호환성을 통해 뒷받침됩니다. 그러나 고령화되는 농업 인구와 농업에 대한 청년층의 최소한의 참여에서 알 수 있듯이 사회적 회복력은 여전히 제한적입니다. 전체적인 시스템 회복력을 강화하기 위해, 카카오 기반 농업에 대한 청년 참여와 지역사회 참여를 촉진하는 표적 개입이 권장됩니다.
summary_3lines: 필리핀 국립공원 인접 지역 농가의 카카오 기반 농업 도입에 따른 지속 가능성과 회복력을 평가하고자 했습니다.
반구조화된 인터뷰와 초점집단 토의, SOC 분석을 통해 카카오 농업이 경제적·생태적 지속 가능성에 기여함을 확인했습니다.
농촌 고령화로 인한 사회적 회복력의 한계를 극복하기 위해 청년층의 참여를 높이는 지역사회 연계형 지원 정책이 필요합니다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구는 기후 취약 지역인 국립공원 주변 농경지에서 카카오 기반 농업 시스템이 지니는 경제적·생태적·사회적 지속 가능성과 회복력을 평가하는 것을 목적으로 합니다. 특히 지역 농가의 소득 다변화와 생태계 적응력 측면에서 카카오 경작의 실효성을 분석하고, 이를 통해 취약한 농업 시스템의 회복력을 높이기 위한 정책적·현장적 개선 방안을 도출하고자 했습니다.
key_findings: 카카오 경작은 농외 소득원 확보와 가족 지원을 통해 농가의 경제적 지속 and 소득 다변화에 기여함

papers.title: Is it the “public” health system? The VOICE model for inclusiveness in universal (national) health systems - lessons from COVID-19
papers.abstract: Since its inception, Israel has provided universal public health care for all its citizens via four not-forprofit health maintenance organizations (HMOs). Definitions of public health abound, including the organized response by society to protect and promote health, to prevent injury, illness, and disability, and to "provide the necessary conditions for a population to be healthy ]1]. Universal or national health systems view the right to health as a human right [2]. Based on that view, the Israel National Health Insurance Law (1994) [3] made health insurance mandatory, stipulating that every resident, irrespective of age, religion, ethnicity, or socio-economic status, is entitled to an exceptionally broad basket of health services [4]. The implementation of the law has indeed increased equality though inequalities still exist [5][6][7][8][9]. Most of the inequality in health policies and services relates to religious minorities such as the Ultra-Orthodox Jews and Muslim Arabs [10][11]. The inequality in a universal system is a major concern of policy makers and health authorities who make continuous efforts to reduce inequalities and shape culturally sensitive policies for planning and delivery of care [4,8,[12][13].A universal health system, by definition, needs to ensure the right to equitable physical and mental health so that rights are not infringed, and policies don't negatively weigh outcomes on both marginalized groups and society [2]. Inequity in the Israeli universal system due to cultural differences has been studied [4,[14][15]. Research on policies and inequalities during COVID-19 and This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article their effect on wellbeing, however, remains remarkably absent [16]. The pandemic generated an opportunity to explore inequity underlying health policies that were applied to the health crisis as a response by policymakers and authorities. The pandemic warrants an exploration of the policies as means of reducing inequities by inclusiveness [15][16].The concept of inclusive health focuses on good health and well-being for everyone. This concept resonates with a rights-based approach to health including political, social, economic, scientific, and cultural actions that are geared toward advancing good health and well-being for all [17]. This study seeks to enhance the understanding of the linkage between health policies during a health crisis, inclusiveness, and inequities, using COVID-19 policies in Israel as a case example. The topic of this study falls within the second group of the basic framework for One Health research which is captured in The World 2050 Initiative (TWI) [18]. This author argues for the need to form inclusive health responses, not only in routine but also during public health emergencies for public health promotion. Insights from this study may inform policy makers and health authorities of universal systems and direct interventions for reducing inequities and ensuring inclusiveness.There are seven religious minorities in Israel comprising 37.5% of the population. In Israel, the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, and the Arab population (Muslim and Christian) are the most prominent and well-defined minority groups [19][20]. According to the Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics 2018, there are three population groups: Jews, who constitute 75% of the population; Arab Israelis, who account for 21% of the population, and others, 4% of the population which include non-Arab Christians, Buddhists, Hindus, Samaritans, and Bahá'ís. In 2015, the Arab Israeli population reached 1.8 M and is comprised of 84% Muslims, 8% Druze, and 8% Christians. Bedouins account for 16% of the Muslim population [21]. These religious minorities are collectivist, and the identity of the group transcends that of the individual [22]. The ultra-Orthodox and Muslim minorities have large families, live in close-knit communities, have death rituals that distinguish them from other marginalized groups, have a complicated relationship with the government, and their behavior is guided by their spiritual leaders [23].Compliance with physical distancing across religious minorities has been shown to be relatively poorer compared to the majority group [22,[24][25]. The Jewish ultra-Orthodox minority comprises 12.6 of the population but 40-60% of all coronavirus patients were Jewish ultra-Orthodox; similarly, the Arab population comprises 21% of the population but 33% of all coronavirus patients were Arab [26]. The social representation theory stresses the need to design culturally adapted messages to reflect the shared reality of each marginalized group [27]. Throughout COVID-19, however, although risk perception has cultural roots, messages calling for physical distancing were not culturally adapted, leading to poor compliance with guidelines [28][29].The COVID-19 pandemic, a public health emergency, affected many countries worldwide. The measures to contain the virus impacted communal traditions and human rights (self-isolation, quarantine, physical distancing, closures), leading to higher stress, distress, family conflicts, and loneliness [30]. Although collective religious practices foster connectedness and resilience, there were no platforms to foster spirituality throughout the adversity faced by minorities 3111-33].Furthermore, minority members claimed that activities in synagogues and mosques, which are critical for spirituality, for social support of bereaved, for family conflict resolution, for marriages, divorces, funerals, and for individual counseling, were banned under the guidelines, without any discussion with spiritual leaders about safe alternatives that had been applied in previous pandemics [34]. Other This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article public places (i.e., parks, bars) were allowed to open whereas places of worship remained closed, leading to disappointment and anger at health authorities and the disengagement of minority members and their leadership from the fight against COVID-19.Due to their poor compliance with guidelines, members of religious minorities, who had to cope with linguistic, employment-related, and socioeconomic challenges, became more vulnerable as it was harder for them to understand and apply public health measures [35]. Members of religious minorities faced heightened discrimination by the majority group [22] The involvement of the police to enforce the health guidelines created fear and a sense of humiliation [32,34]. Reports in the mass media depicted members of religious minorities as lacking respect for the physical distancing measures and jeopardizing public health [36].Media reports also exposed the lack of compliance of the Jewish ultra-Orthodox population with the law mandating hospitalization in public hospitals in cases of severe COVID-19. To avoid having their followers die in solitude, in overflowing, understaffed hospitals, the leadership of the ultra-Orthodox established underground hospitals which were an innovative implementation of patientcentered care in a health crisis [37]. Several month later, the health authorities themselves adapted the policy enabling hospitalization in the community of patients with moderate COVID-19.Moreover, the disempowerment of the religious minority spiritual leaders responsible for the sustainability of their communities during the five waves of the pandemic caused a breach of trust between these communities and the health authorities and inhibited the support of religious leaders for public health measures [34]. COVID-19 guidelines inhibited the practice of death rituals and created multi-level clashes between values and beliefs and guidelines, inhibiting effective processing of grief and effective functioning following loss. Muslims, in particular, experienced disenfranchised grief at the individual and community levels, jeopardizing wellbeing and leading to distrust of authorities and policymakers, deeper polarization in the society, lower utilization of health services, poor mental health, and worsening of chronic illnesses [32,34].Core activities of public health include community education, outbreak investigation and communicable disease control, risk factor and disease surveillance, screening, development and implementation of public health interventions, evaluation, and research. Since the 1970s, public health has been emphasizing the partnership approach, which aims at community engagement, health promotion, and inter-sectoral partnerships [1]. The partnership and collaboration approach throughout COVID-19 in Israel, however, was deficient.Health authorities and policy makers were perceived by members and leaders of religious minorities as failing to recognize the loss of community; as devaluing the spiritual leaders of religious minorities who are responsible for the continuation of community and excluding them from decision making; as unaware of potential adaptations to religious values and beliefs that were possible in previous pandemics; failing to provide resources to help community members plan for practical needs after death; failing to improve wellbeing and resilience through grief counseling and self-care for elders during this challenging time; failing to create and make accessible communication platforms that alleviate anxiety and process collective loss in order to restore social identity [23,32, 34 37-38]. These experiences resulted in distrust, disappointment, and anger at health authorities, rejection of the vaccine, poor compliance with guidelines, ineffective grief, deeper polarization from the majority population, and poor utilization of health services.6 This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article This study explored the inclusiveness of health policies during the pandemic in the Israeli universal health system. The pandemic revealed weaknesses and blind spots in responding to it as a universal health system should. Although reducing inequities by community engagement has been promoted as a key element of epidemic responses, a collaborative approach with minority leaders was found to be lacking [23,32,34,[37][38][39]. Responses to the pandemic exacerbated inequalities that already existed; marginalized underrepresented groups were reported to be left behind and discriminated against partly due to COVID-19 policy responses [2,23,34]. Highlighting the system's blind spots, the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how important it is to ensure an inclusive health approach to health emergencies.Inclusive responses to public health emergencies are a tenet of public universal health systems [17]. Since it was important to balance risks to public safety the insensitivity toward minorities, may have been understandable through the second wave, but from the third wave onward, authorities could have engaged in ongoing negotiations with leaders of religious minorities as the crisis evolved.Lack of inclusion was detrimental to achieving a commitment from minority populations to respect the control measures advocated by public health authorities [40]. As in other countries, health authorities in Israel may have underestimated the capacity of the leadership and of members of these religious minorities to become active in designing the response to the pandemic [41]. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, health responses failed to be empowering and to enhance wellbeing.Voices of minorities were excluded from social discourse and thereby from policy making. Although a public universal system is expected to attend and serve all citizens, this author demonstrated that religious minorities experienced non-inclusive public health responses throughout COVID-19 [2,23,32,34,37].Failing to recognize and address the needs of every marginalized group in the population based on the right to health led to distrust and translated into less compliance, as was demonstrated in Israel by 12% rejection of the first two vaccines, mostly by members of marginalized groups and by 48% rejection of the subsequent boosters [36,42]. If leaders of a marginalized group are excluded from decision making on policy and guidelines, the efficacy of a pandemic response may be severely undermined [41,43]. Exclusionary policies may have a long-term effect on utilization of health services long after the pandemic by neglecting alternative understandings that challenge dominant constructions of health and healthcare [31]. (Campbell et al., 2010). Such neglect weakens the capacity of participatory action to promote transformative change through dialogical orientation [43][44]. Moreover, it may produce or exacerbate health inequities, as policies and services become increasingly adapted to the demands of vocal majorities [45].Participation of leaders of marginalized groups in decision-making foster culturally adapted policies which make more responsive policies, and, consequently, healthier populations [46].Initiatives that focus on community empowerment are increasingly prominent in public health policy . However, while participation and inclusion are necessary conditions for empowerment, attention to the breadth of inclusion and to the extent to which it is experienced as empowering was insufficient [47]. Several recommendations are proposed to promote inclusiveness in responses of universal systems to a health crisis.Health authorities have a role in promoting the substantive inclusion of marginalized groups in healthcare decision-making [43]. Health authorities must be strategic and proactive in reaching out to specific groups, to identify and address their needs, to disseminate transparent and accurate public health information, and shape actionable options to enhance public trust in health authorities and policymakers [41]. Actively listening to leaders of religious minorities can facilitate collaborations with the communities which will reduce tensions through the process of reclaiming trust in This is a provisional file, not the final typeset article authorities and policy makers. A collaborative approach may lead to open conversations that elucidate the challenges that religious minorities experience and the effects on equity and public health principles, especially in universal health systems.There are implications for policy makers and authorities at three levels: Leadership, community levels, and collaborators. At the leadership level, to establish trust of leaders and their communities, in authorities, health authorities must validate the leadership of minorities by approaching it , initiating dialogues, providing transparent empirical data, and understanding disparities in approach and objections. Authorities and policymakers should avoid top-down imposition of solutions using a one-size-fits-all model [48]. At the community level, authorities are called upon to understand the sources of objection and distrust and use culturally appropriate channels to communicate. Regarding collaborators, this author proposes to engage clinicians from religious minorities and collaborate with them to initiate community-based efforts to understand their needs, concerns, and possible solutions.To succeed in promoting inclusiveness, authorities, and policy makers should apply the VOICE model in several steps. First explore their Values regarding inclusiveness in universal health systems.Second, be Open: the knowledge does not lie only with policymakers. Reflect and ask what we learned during COVID-19. Although there is a universal health system that aspires to eliminate inequities, state policies in practice reduced inclusiveness and enhanced perceived and actual inequities between the majority population and religious minorities. Third, Inquire about needs, concerns, objections of minorities. Fourth, Communicate and Collaborate to develop possible culturally adapted alternatives to the policies to preserve public health on the one hand and to respond in a way that includes religious minorities, on the other. Fifth, Explore alternatives over time. Figure 1 presents the VOICE model. Looking forward, health authorities may intervene to ensure inclusiveness in health services for all members of society. Ensuring inclusive health responses is important in addressing health inequities in the short and long term [49]. This author proposes six interventions to foster inclusiveness: a.Create future inclusiveness through leadership education making sure that the health authority boards that make policy decisions reflect the diversity of the population. b. Train the next generations of leaders by inclusive communication, public engagement, involved networks, as well as recruiting agents from each minority and setting up advisory groups. With time these measures will help the leaders of religious minorities to gain influence to shape policies and help reclaim trust in policymakers health authorities. c. Employ measures to prevent the infringement of civil rights of minorities and assess it as an important measure for health quality d. Reward practices of inclusiveness to direct conduct toward this goal. e. Critically appraise practice by evaluating and measuring trust, polarization, and utilization of health services. This is a provisional file, not the final typeset articleInclusive, dynamic, multi-stakeholder, responses of health systems remain critical in the context of health emergencies. Responses of public health authorities and health systems, are to be more strategic, proactive, and inclusive, reaching out to all minorities and addressing their specific needs, values, and beliefs. Such an inclusive health approach may foster solidarity and health equity, perhaps leading to more effective responses of religious minorities to public health interventions in both emergencies and routine. Shaping strategies to target diverse multi-stakeholders is a first step to engage everyone in society, reduce discrimination, health inequity, and health deterioration. A commitment to an inclusive system implies that activities and responses will be sensitive to all. This maintains the commitment of health systems to be universal health systems, for everyone, including in emergencies. As the COVID-19 pandemic, an unprecedented humanitarian crisis, continues to threaten and impact public health systems around the world, disrupting the well-being of people, inclusiveness in public health universal systems, cannot only exist in declarations. Inclusiveness cannot be overlooked. Policies should link policymakers and public health authorities with members and leaders of religious minorities to better respond to the needs of all.

ai_analysis.title_ko: 이것이 진정한 '공공' 보건 체계인가? 보편적(국가) 보건 체계의 포용성을 위한 VOICE 모델 - 코로나19의 교훈
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 이스라엘은 건국 이래 4개의 비영리 건강관리기구를 통해 모든 시민에게 보편적인 공공 보건 의료를 제공해왔습니다. 이스라엘 국가건강보험법(1994)은 모든 거주자가 연령, 종교, 인종, 사회경제적 지위와 상관없이 폭넓은 보건 서비스를 받을 권리가 있음을 규정하여 평등성을 높였으나, 초정통파 유대인이나 무슬림 아랍인 같은 종교적 소수자 사이에서는 여전히 불평등이 존재합니다. 보편적 시스템 내의 이러한 불평등은 정책 결정자와 보건 당국이 문화적으로 민감한 정책을 형성하고 불평등을 줄이기 위해 지속적인 노력을 기울이게 만드는 주요 관심사입니다. 코로나19 팬데믹은 위기 상황에서 소외된 집단과 사회 전체에 부정적인 영향을 미치는 보건 정책의 기저에 깔린 불평등을 탐색할 수 있는 기회를 제공했습니다. 포용적 보건의 개념은 모든 사람의 건강과 웰빙을 증진하는 것을 목표로 하며, 이는 정치적, 사회적, 경제적, 문화적 조치를 포함하는 권리 기반 접근 방식과 일치합니다. 본 연구는 이스라엘의 코로나19 정책을 사례 연구로 활용하여 보건 위기 시의 보건 정책, 포용성, 불평등 간의 연관성에 대한 이해를 높이고자 합니다. 연구 결과는 보건 당국이 평상시뿐만 아니라 공중보건 비상사태 시에도 포용적인 보건 대응을 마련하여 불평등을 줄이고 건강권을 보장하는 데 기여할 수 있는 통찰을 제공합니다.
summary_3lines: 이스라엘의 코로나19 보건 정책 사례를 통해 공중보건 위기 상황에서 보편적 보건 체계가 마주하는 포용성과 불평등의 문제를 분석하고자 했다.
팬데믹 대응 과정에서 종교적 소수자 등 소외 계층이 겪는 건강 불평등과 문화적 요인의 영향을 검토했다.
공중보건 비상사태 시 소외 계층을 배제하지 않는 포용적 정책 수립과 관리 체계 개선의 필요성을 시사한다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구는 이스라엘의 코로나19 대응 보건 정책을 사례로 삼아, 보편적 보건 체계 내에서 위기 상황 발생 시 나타나는 포용성과 불평등의 상관관계, 그리고 소외 계층에 대한 정책적 영향력의 한계를 분석하는 것을 목적으로 합니다. 평상시는 물론 공중보건 비상사태 시에도 모든 구성원에게 공평한 보건 혜택이 돌아갈 수 있도록 하는 포용적 정책 모델의 필요성을 강조하고자 합니다.
key_findings: 보편적 보건 체계를 표방하더라도 문화적, 종교적 소수자 집단은 위기 상황에서 의료 서비스 접근성 및 건강 형평성 측면에서 불이익을 겪을 수 있다.
코로나19와 같은 공중보건 비상사태는 기존 보건 정책에 내재된 불평등을 증폭시키며, 획일적인 정책 적용은 소외 계층의 건강권을 침해할 수 있다.
모든 계층의 건강과 웰빙을 보장하기 위해서는 정치, 사회, 문화적 다양성을 고려한 포용적이고 민감한 정책 설계가 필수적이다.
practical_applications: 국립공원 내 재난 및 감염병 등 비상사태 대응 매뉴얼 수립 시, 외국인, 고령자, 장애인 등 소외·취약 탐방객의 특성을 반영한 맞춤형 안내 체계를 구축한다.
탐방객 안전 및 복지 서비스 제공에 있어 문화적·신체적 장벽을 허물고, 모든 국민이 차별 없이 국립공원의 혜택을 누릴 수 있도록 포용적 운영 지침을 마련한다.
공원 내 다중이용시설 및 프로그램 운영 시 사회적 약자의 접근성을 사전에 점검하고 보완하는 모니터링 프로세스를 도입한다.
ai_analysis.korea_np_applicability_reason: 본 논문은 의료 보건 체계와 사회적 불평등을 다룬 공중보건학 연구로, 국립공원의 직접적인 생태 관리나 탐방로 운영보다는 보편적 공공 서비스의 포용성이라는 거버넌스 관점에 가깝기 때문에 국립공원 현장 적용성은 상대적으로 낮습니다.
field_checklist: 재난 및 비상 상황 발생 시 취약계층(고령자, 장애인 등)을 위한 대피 안내 체계가 마련되어 있는가?
공원 내 탐방 프로그램 및 편의시설 이용에 있어 언어적·문화적 장벽을 겪는 소외 방문객이 존재하는지 확인했는가?
공공 서비스 제공 시 모든 탐방객이 동등한 혜택과 안전을 보장받도록 설계된 운영 지침이 현장에 배포되었는가?
비상 대응 계획 수립 과정에서 다양한 사용자 집단의 의견이 수렴되고 반영되었는가?
취약 계층의 공원 접근성 실태를 주기적으로 점검하고 미비점을 개선하고 있는가?
cautions: 의료 보건 분야의 이론적 모델(VOICE 모델 등)을 국립공원 탐방객 안전 관리 현장에 무리하게 직접 대입하는 것은 제한이 따를 수 있습니다.
국내 국립공원의 여건에 맞는 법적 근거와 현장 실무 지침과의 연계성을 면밀히 검토해야 합니다.
recommended_followup_research: 국립공원 탐방 및 재난 안전 서비스 이용 시 사회적 취약계층이 겪는 불평등 실태 조사
자연공원 내 공공 서비스의 형평성과 포용적 거버넌스 구축 방안 연구

ai_analysis.title_ko: NIEHS 워크숍: 환경 보건 연구를 위한 독창적인 해양 및 담수 생물 모델
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 본 논문은 환경 보건 연구에서 해양 및 담수 생물 모델의 중요성을 다룬 미국 국립환경보건과학연구소(NIEHS) 워크숍의 결과물입니다. 다양한 수생 생물 모델이 독성물질 노출, 내분비계 교란 물질, 그리고 환경 오염이 생태계와 생물에 미치는 영향을 평가하는 데 어떻게 활용될 수 있는지 논의합니다. 특히 어류 및 기타 수생 생물을 활용한 유전적, 발달적 독성 연구의 필요성을 강조하고 있습니다.
summary_3lines: 환경 보건 연구에서 해양 및 담수 생물 모델의 활용 가능성과 중요성을 조명하기 위해 워크숍이 개최되었습니다.
다양한 수생 생물 모델을 통해 환경 오염물질과 내분비계 교란 물질의 독성 평가 및 유전적 영향 분석 결과가 공유되었습니다.
수생 생물 모델은 향후 국립공원 내 수계 환경 오염 모니터링 및 생태계 건강성 평가 체계 구축에 활용될 수 있습니다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 환경 보건 연구에서 해양 및 담수 생물 모델의 활용 가치를 평가하고, 수생 생물을 이용한 독성학적 연구 방법론을 공유하고자 하였습니다.
key_findings: 수생 생물 모델은 환경 내 내분비계 교란 물질의 영향을 평가하는 데 매우 유용합니다.
어류 배아 등을 활용한 발달 독성 평가는 오염물질의 생태적 위해성을 조기에 탐지하는 데 기여합니다.
분자 및 유전 독성학적 접근을 통해 수생 생물에 미치는 미세 오염원의 영향을 정밀하게 분석할 수 있습니다.
practical_applications: 국립공원 내 하천 및 호소 등 수계 환경 조사를 위한 생물학적 모니터링 지표 선정에 참고합니다.
수생 생물을 활용한 환경 독성 및 수질 오염 영향 평가 기법을 공원 관리 실무에 도입합니다.
내분비계 교란 물질 등 신종 오염원이 공원 내 수생태계에 미치는 영향 분석을 위한 연구 과제를 기획합니다.
ai_analysis.korea_np_applicability_reason: 기초 의학 및 독성학적 실험실 연구 중심의 내용으로, 국립공원 현장 관리 실무에 직접 적용하기에는 거리가 있으나 수계 생태계 건강성 평가 및 모니터링의 이론적 배경으로 일부 활용할 수 있습니다.
related_laws: 야생생물 보호 및 관리에 관한 법률 제8조
field_checklist: 국립공원 내 주요 수계의 수질 및 수생태계 건강성 지표 정기 확인
수생 생물상 변화 모니터링 계획 수립 여부 점검
상류 지역 오염원 유입에 따른 수생 생물 영향 조사
공원 내 하천 생태계 보호를 위한 수질 오염 감시 체계 점검
수생 생물 지표를 활용한 환경 모니터링 장비 및 인력 현황 파악
cautions: 실험실 기반의 독성 연구 결과이므로 야외 국립공원 현장에 즉시 적용하기에는 한계가 있습니다.
수생 생물 채집 및 조사는 관련 법령에 따른 허가와 절차를 준수해야 합니다.
recommended_followup_research: 국립공원 수계 내 미량 오염물질이 수생 생물에 미치는 영향에 관한 현장 중심 연구
한국 국립공원 수생태계 건강성 평가를 위한 지표 종 발굴 및 모니터링 기법 고도화

papers.title: Sports cardiology: the benefits of cardiorespiratory fitness in young adults, the elderly, and patients with arrythmias
papers.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. We all know that exercise is good and sitting around is bad. However, major issues in sports cardiology remain unsolved: is cardiorespiratory fitness at a young age of benefit for a person’s entire lifetime and is taking up regular physical activity at an older age still useful or a waste of time? Finally, is exercise harmful for certain cardiac patients? In patients with arrythmogenic1 or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy,2 vigorous exercise may be particularly harmful. Accordingly, recommendations for cardiac patients have been published.3 That atrial fibrillation confers a higher risk of morbidity and mortality is common knowledge,4 but the long-term impact of physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness on outcomes in atrial fibrillation is unknown. Of note, vigorous exercise may increase the risk of this arrythmia.5 This topic is addressed in the first article ‘Physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with atrial fibrillation: the HUNT study’ by Bjarne Martens Nes and colleagues from the University of Medicine in Trondheim in Norway.6 They examined the impact of physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness on all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, morbidity, and stroke in individuals with atrial fibrillation. Nes and colleagues followed 1117 atrial fibrillation patients from the HUNT3 study in 2006–2008 until first occurrence of outcomes or end of follow-up in November 2015. They used Cox proportional hazard regression to examine the prospective associations of self-reported physical activity and estimated cardiorespiratory fitness with the outcomes. Atrial fibrillation patients meeting physical activity guidelines had a lower risk of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, compared with inactive patients, with hazard ratios of 0.55 and 0.54, respectively (Figure 1). The respective hazard ratios for cardiovascular morbidity and stroke were 0.78 and 0.70. Each 1-metabolic equivalent task (MET) higher estimated cardiorespiratory fitness was associated with a lower risk of all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality and morbidity, with hazard ratios between 0.85 and 0.88. Thus, higher physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness are associated with lower long-term risk of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality even in individuals with atrial fibrillation, supporting regular physical activity and improved cardiorespiratory fitness in such patients. These novel findings are put into context in a thought-provoking Editorial by Dariush Mozaffarian from the Friedman School of Nutrition Science & Policy in Boston, Massachusetts, USA.7 Survival probabilities for all-cause and CVD mortality according to physical activity level among individuals with atrial fibrillation (from Garnvik LE, Malmo V, Janszky I, Ellekjær H, Wisløff U, Loennechen JP, Nes BM. Physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with atrial fibrillation: the HUNT study. See pages 1467–1475). Adrian Elliott and colleagues from the University of Adelaide in South Australia looked at this issue from another angle. It is known that physical activity reduces cardiovascular disease burden, but its impact not only on supraventricular, but also on the more serious ventricular arrhythmias is less certain. They address this in their article entitled ‘Association between physical activity and risk of incident arrhythmias in 402 406 individuals: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort’.8 They studied 402 406 individuals, half of them female (with >2.8 million person-years of follow-up), who underwent self-reported physical activity assessment computed in metabolic equivalent-minutes per week (MET-min/week) at baseline and detailed physical assessment and medical history. Incident atrial fibrillation risk was lower amongst physically active participants, with a more pronounced reduction amongst female participants than males. Similarly, there was a lower risk of ventricular arrhythmias amongst physically active participants that remained relatively stable over a broad range of physical activity levels. Vigorous physical activity was also associated with reduced ventricular arrhythmia risk. Total or vigorous physical activity were not associated with bradyarrhythmias. Thus, the risk of atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias is lower amongst physically active individuals, findings that are further discussed in an Editorial by Stanley Nattel from the University of Montreal in Quebec, Canada.9 Little is known about the association of changes in moderate to vigorous physical activity level with cardiovascular disease, especially in older adults whose ability to engage in frequent moderate or vigorous exercise naturally wanes with age. In their article ‘Changes in exercise frequency and cardiovascular outcomes in older adults’ Sang Min Park and colleagues from the Seoul National University Hospital in South Korea examined the association between moderate to vigorous physical activity and cardiovascular disease in >1.1 million adults aged 60 years or older.10 Compared with those who were continuously physically inactive, those who increased their frequency of moderate to vigorous physical activity from physically inactive to 1–2 times per week had a significantly reduced risk for cardiovascular disease. Older adults who became physically inactive from engaging in more than 1–2 times of activity per week had a higher cardiovascular risk compared with those who maintained their frequency of moderate to vigorous physical activity. Thus, among older adults, engaging in a higher frequency of moderate to vigorous physical activity or maintaining the level was associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease. These clinically highly relevant findings particularly in ageing affluent societies are further discussed an Editorial by Sanjay Sharma from the St George’s University of London, UK.11 Cardiorespiratory fitness,12 muscular strength,13 and obesity14,15 in adulthood are risk factors for future cardiovascular disease. However, little is known regarding the associations of these risk factors, already in adolescence, with later disability due to chronic cardiovascular disease. In their manuscript entitled ‘Cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and obesity in adolescence and later chronic disability due to cardiovascular disease: a cohort study of 1 million men’, Hanna Henriksson and colleagues from the Linköping University in Linköping, Sweden investigated associations of cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and body mass index in adolescence with later chronic disability due to specific causes of cardiovascular disease disability, i.e. cerebrovascular disease, ischaemic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, and heart failure.16 This population-based cohort study included 1 078 685 male adolescents aged 16–19 years from the Swedish military conscription register. Cardiorespiratory fitness on the bicycle ergometer, muscular strength assessed by knee extension strength, and body mass index were measured. Information about disability pension due to cardiovascular disease was retrieved from the Social Insurance Agency during a mean follow-up of 28.4 years. Cardiorespiratory fitness was strongly and inversely associated with later risk of chronic cardiovascular disease disability for all investigated causes. The association was particularly strong for ischaemic heart diseases, with a hazard ratio of 0.11 for the highest compared with the lowest fitness quintiles. Furthermore, overweight or obesity was associated with cardiovascular disability for all investigated causes (Figure 2). Conversely, associations of muscular strength with cardiovascular disease disability were generally weak. Thus, this study provides evidence for associations between low levels of cardiorespiratory fitness and obesity with later risk of chronic disability due to cardiovascular disease. Preventive actions therefore should begin at a young age and include promotion of cardiorespiratory fitness and healthy body weight. These findings are put into context in an interesting Editorial by John Deanfield from the Institute of Child Health in London, UK.17 Combined association of cardiorespiratory fitness and body mass index at conscription with a disability pension due to cardiovascular diseases. NW, normal weight (n = 879 045); OB, obesity (n = 17 913). Adolescents with fitness in quintile 1 were considered as ‘Unfit’ while adolescents in quintiles 2–5 were considered ‘Fit’. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Models were adjusted for age, centre, year of conscription, childhood socioeconomic position, and muscular strength at conscription (from Henriksson H, Henriksson P, Tynelius P, Ekstedt M, Berglind D, Labayen I, Ruiz JR, Lavie CJ, Ortega FB. Cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and obesity in adolescence and later chronic disability due to cardiovascular disease: a cohort study of 1 million men. See pages 1503–1510). Sport may even favourably affect ageing, one of the most important underlying molecular pathways of cardiovascular disease. In this context, important pathways are ageing18 and longevity genes,19,20 as well as telomerase activity. For instance, endurance training and interval training, but not resistance training, increase telomerase activity and telomere length which are important for cellular senescence, regenerative capacity, and thus healthy ageing.21 A surrogate circulation to investigate such mechanisms is the easily accessible retinal circulation.22 Indeed, retinal vessel diameters are associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).23 Promoter DNA methylation is a repressor of transcription of the mitochondrial adaptor p66Shc gene, a key driver of ageing-induced reactive oxygen species. In an EHJ Brief Communication entitled ‘High-intensity interval training modulates retinal microvascular phenotype and DNA methylation of p66Shc gene: a randomized controlled trial (EXAMIN AGE)’, Francesco Cosentino and colleagues from the University Hospital Solna in Stockholm, Sweden aimed to investigate whether high-intensity interval training affects retinal microvascular phenotype as well as p66Shc expression and oxidative stress in ageing subjects with increased cardiovascular risk from the EXAMIN AGE cohort.24 Eighty-four sedentary subjects with two or more cardiovascular risk factors were randomized into either a 12-week high-intensity interval training or standard recommendations. Retinal arteriolar and venular diameters were measured by use of a retinal vessel analyser. As a marker of oxidative stress, plasma 3-nitrotyrosine level was determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). High-intensity interval training reduced body mass index, fat mass, and LDL, and increased muscle mass as well as maximal oxygen uptake. Moreover, high-intensity interval training restored the microvascular phenotype by inducing retinal arteriolar widening and venular narrowing. After high-intensity interval training, restoration of p66Shc promoter methylation reduced p66Shc gene expression and, in turn, blunted 3-nitrotyrosine plasma levels. Thus, high-intensity interval training rescues microvascular dysfunction in ageing subjects at increased cardiovascular risk. Exercise-induced reprogramming of DNA methylation of the p66Shc gene may represent a putative mechanistic link whereby exercise protects against age-related oxidative stress. The issue is complemented by various Discussion Forum pieces. In a contribution entitled ‘Triglyceride lowering drugs: not just icosapent ethyl’ J. David Spence and colleagues from the Robarts Research Institute in London Ontario, Canada comment on the recent publication ‘Real-world risk of cardiovascular outcomes associated with hypertriglyceridaemia among individuals with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and potential eligibility for emerging therapies’ by Patrick Lawler and colleagues from the Toronto General Hospital in Ontario, Canada.25,26 Lawler et al. respond in a separate contribution.27 In a further Discussion Forum entitled ‘Acrolein exposure from electronic cigarettes’, Bernd Mayer from the Karl-Franzens-Universitat Graz in Austria comment on the recent publication entitled ‘Short-term e-cigarette vapour exposure causes vascular oxidative stress and dysfunction: evidence for a close connection to brain damage and a key role of the phagocytic NADPH oxidase (NOX-2)’ by Thomas Münzel and colleagues from the Johannes Gutenberg Universität from Mainz, Germany.28,29 Münzel et al. respond in a separate contribution.30 In a final contribution entitled ‘Acute vs. chronic effects of e-cigarettes on vascular function’ Konstantinos Farsalinos from the Onassis Cardiac Surgery Center in Kallithea, Greece comment on the same contribution by Münzel et al.29,31 Münzel et al. also respond to this comment in a separate piece.32 The editors hope that readers of this issue of the European Heart Journal will find it of interest. With thanks to Amelia Meier-Batschelet for help with compilation of this article.

ai_analysis.title_ko: 스포츠 심장학: 젊은 성인, 노인, 부정맥 환자에서 심폐 체력의 이점
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 운동이 몸에 좋고 앉아있는 생활이 해롭다는 것은 누구나 잘 알고 있습니다. 그러나 스포츠 심장학의 주요 과제들은 여전히 해결되지 않았습니다. 즉, 젊은 시절의 심폐 체력이 평생 동안 유익한지, 고령에 시작하는 규칙적인 신체활동이 여전히 유용한지 아니면 시간 낭비인지에 대한 것입니다. 마지막으로, 운동이 특정 심장 환자에게 해를 끼치는지에 대한 의문도 있습니다. 부정맥유발성 또는 비대성 심근병증 환자에게 고강도 운동은 특히 해로울 수 있으므로, 심장 환자를 위한 권고사항이 발표된 바 있습니다. 심방세동이 이병률과 사망률의 위험을 높인다는 것은 상식이나, 신체활동과 심폐 체력이 심방세동 환자의 예후에 미치는 장기적 영향은 아직 알려지지 않았습니다. 특히 고강도 운동은 이 부정맥의 위험을 증가시킬 수 있습니다. 이 주제는 노르웨이 트론헤임 의대의 비야르네 마르텐스 네스(Bjarne Martens Nes) 연구팀이 발표한 첫 번째 논문인 '심방세동 환자에서의 신체활동, 심폐 체력, 그리고 심혈관 예후: HUNT 연구'에서 다루어지고 있습니다. 그들은 심방세동 환자들을 대상으로 신체활동과 심폐 체력이 모든 원인에 의한 사망률, 심혈관 사망률, 이병률 및 뇌졸중에 미치는 영향을 조사했습니다. 연구팀은 2006~2008년 HUNT3 연구의 심방세동 환자 1,117명을 첫 번째 결과 발생 또는 2015년 11월 추적 관찰 종료 시점까지 추적 조사했습니다. 자가 보고된 신체활동과 추정된 심폐 체력이 예후와 맺는 전향적 연관성을 조사하기 위해 콕스 비례 위험 회귀 분석을 사용했습니다. 신체활동 지침을 충족하는 심방세동 환자는 비활동적인 환자에 비해 모든 원인 및 심혈관 사망률 위험이 낮았으며, 위험비는 각각 0.55와 0.54였습니다. 심혈관 이병률과 뇌졸중에 대한 각각의 위험비는 0.78과 0.70이었습니다. 추정된 심폐 체력이 대사당량(MET) 기준으로 1단위 높을 때마다 모든 원인 및 심혈관 질환 사망률과 이병률의 위험 감소와 연관되었으며, 위험비는 0.85에서 0.88 사이였습니다. 따라서 신체활동과 심폐 체력의 증가는 심방세동 환자에게서조차 심혈관 및 모든 원인에 의한 사망률의 장기적 위험 감소와 연관되어 있으며, 이는 해당 환자들에게 규칙적인 신체활동과 심폐 체력 향상을 뒷받침합니다.
summary_3lines: 본 연구는 신체활동과 심폐 체력이 심방세동 환자의 사망률과 심혈관 질환 발생에 미치는 장기적 영향을 규명하기 위해 수행되었습니다.
노르웨이 HUNT3 연구의 심방세동 환자 1,117명을 대상으로 분석한 결과, 운동 지침을 충족하는 환자는 비활동적 환자에 비해 사망 및 뇌졸중 위험이 유의하게 낮았습니다.
부정맥 환자라 하더라도 적절한 신체활동과 심폐 체력 향상은 사망 위험을 줄이는 데 기여하므로 맞춤형 탐방 및 운동 프로그램 운영 시 실무적으로 참고해야 합니다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구의 목적은 신체활동과 심폐 체력이 심방세동을 앓고 있는 환자들의 모든 원인에 의한 사망률, 심혈관 사망률, 이병률, 그리고 뇌졸중 발생에 미치는 장기적인 영향을 파악하는 것입니다. 특히 고령층이나 심장 질환자가 운동을 할 때의 안전성과 이점을 검증하고자 하였습니다.
key_findings: 신체활동 지침을 준수한 심방세동 환자는 비활동 환자에 비해 모든 원인에 의한 사망 위험이 45% 낮았음.
심혈관 사망률 위험 또한 신체활동을 한 환자군에서 46% 낮게 나타남.
심폐 체력이 1 MET 증가할 때마다 심혈관 질환 사망 및 이병 위험이 12%에서 15% 가량 감소함.
practical_applications: 고령 탐방객 및 심혈관 질환 이력이 있는 탐방객을 위한 맞춤형 저·중강도 탐방 코스를 개발하고 안내합니다.
국립공원 탐방 안내소 및 안전관리반에서 탐방객의 체력 수준에 맞는 안전한 탐방 활동 가이드를 제공합니다.
탐방객 응급 상황 발생 시 신속한 대처를 위해 주요 탐방로 입구에 심장충전기(AED) 등 응급 안전시설을 확충합니다.
ai_analysis.korea_np_applicability_reason: 본 논문은 의료 데이터를 기반으로 한 심장 질환 환자의 임상 연구이므로 국립공원 생태계나 지형 관리에 직접 적용되기는 어렵습니다. 다만, 고령 탐방객과 만성질환자의 안전사고 예방 및 건강증진 탐방 프로그램 운영에는 간접적으로 유용합니다.
field_checklist: 주요 탐방로 입구 및 거점 지역에 자동심장충전기(AED)가 정상 작동하는지 확인
고령 및 심혈관 질환 탐방객을 위한 안전 수칙 및 비상 연락망 안내판 정비
탐방로 경사도 및 난이도에 따른 체력 소모량(METs 등) 추정 정보 제공 여부 점검
응급 환자 발생 시 공원 관리사무소와 지역 소방·의료 기관 간 비상 연락 체계 가동 상태 확인
탐방객 대상 자율 건강 체크(혈압 측정 등) 부스나 프로그램 운영 여부 점검
cautions: 심장 질환이 있는 탐방객에게 무리한 고강도 산행이나 탐방을 유도하지 않도록 주의해야 합니다.
의학적 전문 지식이 필요한 건강 조언보다는 안전한 탐방 유도와 응급 대응 체계 구축에 집중해야 합니다.
recommended_followup_research: 국립공원 탐방객의 연령별·질환별 체력 수준에 따른 탐방로 난이도 적합성 평가 연구
자연 속 신체활동이 탐방객의 심혈관 건강 및 정신 건강에 미치는 단기·장기 효과 분석

papers.title: Advancing rural aging policy in California: recommendations for state policy on housing, long-term services and supports, and health care access
papers.abstract: Rural communities are aging faster than urban and suburban areas and bear a higher burden of disability and chronic conditions, intensifying demand for long-term services and supports (LTSS), accessible housing, and health care (Cohen & Greaney, 2023; Monnat, 2025). This demand collides with longstanding structural constraints: geographic isolation, workforce shortages, chronic underinvestment, and thin service infrastructures that disadvantage low-density regions where distance and limited capacity make uniform policy models less feasible (Bennett et al., 2019; Rhubart et al., 2021). Together, these cross-domain challenges define a persistent rural aging equity gap. California’s Multisector Plan for Aging (MPA), known as the Master Plan for Aging, is a model now adopted or explored by 37 states, offering a pivotal platform to coordinate across sectors (West Health, 2024). However, translating statewide frameworks into equitable outcomes for rural communities requires intentional engagement and policy adaptation. In 2022, The SCAN Foundation launched the Rural MPA Initiative, supporting coalitions across three rural regions spanning seven counties. Grounded in collective impact and community-engaged research principles (National Academy of Medicine, 2022), regional coalitions convened cross-sector advisory committees and engaged residents historically underrepresented in planning and policy processes. Over three years, 227 community members and professionals provided qualitative input through focus groups, listening sessions, and interviews. This input was coupled with secondary data to identify barriers and develop locally grounded action plans. Translating statewide frameworks into equitable outcomes for rural communities requires intentional engagement and policy adaptation. In 2025, community-identified challenges and recommendations from the three regions were synthesized and refined through iterative consultation with 82 state and local experts, including advocacy organizations, government agencies, and rural providers, resulting in the Rural Aging in California: Policy Brief Series focused on long-term services and supports (LTSS), housing, and health care access (DeLange Martinez et al., 2025a). This article describes the cross-domain challenges identified by rural older adults, caregivers, and providers and presents corresponding implementation-oriented policy recommendations codeveloped with state and local experts and adapted for other states. Although grounded in California, this approach provides a replicable model for ensuring that state MPAs reflect unique local needs, resulting in more inclusive plans. Long-term services and supports (LTSS) encompass the spectrum of paid and unpaid assistance such as personal care, medication management, and specialized housing or community programs that people with disabilities and chronic conditions need over time. LTSS includes home and community-based services (HCBS), institutional facilities, and caregiver support. In rural California, these services are fragmented and difficult to navigate, placing an immense burden on older adults, individuals with disabilities, and family caregivers. A significant disconnect exists between formal policy language describing LTSS and the lived experiences of rural community members. Three structural barriers are particularly salient: insufficient support for family caregivers, complex and difficult-to-navigate systems, and an unstable direct care workforce. Limited awareness of available programs and services, uncertainty about eligibility, and cultural norms of self-reliance reduce service use even when programs exist. Low wages, long travel distances, limited training, and high turnover among direct care workers reinforce service instability and caregiver burden, leaving many rural older adults to rely solely on informal networks or to forego care altogether. Table 1 summarizes the structural barriers shaping rural LTSS challenges and the corresponding state policy recommendations developed to address them. Some recommendations could apply to more than one challenge (see also DeLange Martinez et al., 2025b). Long-term services and supports: challenges and policy recommendations. Expand Older Americans Act (OAA) caregiver support programs (respite, education, counseling) Conduct targeted outreach to help caregivers self-identify Expand Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) options that allow payment of family caregivers, with rural-specific training and navigation supports Simplify enrollment and recertification processes Strengthen Aging and Disability Resource Connections (ADRCs) as single points of entry Fund case management for individuals just above Medicaid eligibility Support enrollment across Medicaid and state-funded HCBS Fund benefits counseling and caregiver education Pilot bridge supports and relocation assistance for near-eligible households Identify new revenue sources to fund a statewide long-term care benefit Establish a statewide direct care workforce registry, beginning in rural areas Establish tiered wage scales for specialized certifications and higher-acuity care (e.g., dementia, behavioral health) Reimburse travel time and mileage, including travel from workers’ to clients’ homes Align Medicaid and non-Medicaid HCBS reimbursement rates with the true cost of rural service delivery Establish competitive, tiered wages that reflect the complexity of care provided Expand benefits (health care, paid leave, retirement) Offer retention incentives Develop portable benefits that paid workers retain across employers and care settings Invest in rural workforce stabilization funds Establish career advancement pathways with compensated peer mentorship and training roles Establish statewide direct care worker advisory councils with meaningful rural representation Scale modular training through rural community colleges and workforce partnerships Fund stipends, tuition, and device/connectivity support for family caregivers Expand rural access to dementia- and disability-specific training These challenges echo established research indicating that rural LTSS are often fragmented and rely heavily on families (Coburn & Lundblad, 2017; Henning-Smith & Lahr, 2018). Family caregiving is more prevalent in rural areas and frequently occurs without support from formal systems (Miller et al., 2023). Geographic isolation, limited transportation, and workforce shortages constrain access to paid home care, intensifying reliance on community and church networks (Dill et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2023; Patano et al., 2024). Direct care workforce shortages are more severe in rural settings, where high turnover and limited training undermine HCBS delivery (Kallas et al., 2023). The policy recommendations in Table 1 emphasize scaling and adapting established programs and tools such as Medicaid HCBS, Older Americans Act programs, and workforce investments to account for rural geography and capacity constraints. Prioritizing adaptation and integration of existing programs enhances feasibility in rural settings, where long travel distances, limited infrastructure (including public transportation), and workforce instability directly affect service delivery and reliability. Housing functions as a foundational determinant of rural older adults’ ability to age safely and remain in their communities. Housing is inextricably linked to health outcomes and caregiving capacity; instability after an illness or disaster can trigger a cascade of crises for older adults and their caregivers. The rural housing system is under strain: fixed incomes are outpaced by rising costs, accessible homes are scarce, navigation barriers are complex, and vulnerability to displacement from disasters or eviction is acute. Furthermore, distance and transportation constraints dictate which housing options are feasible, and gaps in services and case management make it harder to remain safely housed when care needs increase. Table 2 summarizes the primary community-identified challenges within the housing domain and the corresponding state policy recommendations developed to address them through affordability, supply, housing quality, navigation, and cross-system coordination (see also DeLange Martinez et al., 2025c). Housing stability for rural older adults: from community-identified challenges to policy recommendations. Target housing and homelessness resources to older adults Require local housing plans to address the needs of low-income older adults and require local jurisdictions to allocate dedicated funding for adults 55+ Expand flexible housing pools to braid funding across housing, aging, and health systems and stabilize housing during transitions Expand tax credits, bonds, and grants to develop and preserve affordable senior housing Increase incentives for rural landlord participation in housing vouchers Expand home-sharing programs Increase permanent supportive housing in rural areas Promote co-location of affordable housing with onsite services like adult day centers, case management, and transportation services Expand funding for home repair, accessibility, and climate-resilient retrofits Expand home modification program eligibility to include manufactured and mobile homes Fund infrastructure upgrades in Mobile Home Parks to support safe aging in place Fund flexible rural transportation models (e.g., volunteer drivers, on-demand services) Support mobility management programs Invest in community centers that co-locate services to reduce travel burden Make permanent and scale housing navigation and stabilization programs, including Medicaid-supported housing services and state-funded homelessness prevention initiatives Increase rural funding for case management, navigation, and flexible financial assistance that can be deployed quickly during transitions Strengthen rental protections and enforcement in rural areas Expand funding for eviction prevention and culturally and linguistically accessible legal aid Deploy mobile legal clinics and authorize Community Justice Workers in rural areas Reform homelessness data systems to capture hidden homelessness in rural areas Require age-disaggregated reporting across housing and homelessness programs Integrate housing data with Adult Protective Services (APS) and aging services Track outcomes by age, gender, race, ethnicity, and geography to surface rural disparities Strengthen coordination among Continuums of Care, Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs), ADRCs, APS, Centers for Independent Living, Housing Authorities, and Medicaid programs Align accountability across systems through shared protocols, referral pathways, and information sharing Fund disaster navigation for older adults Simplify disaster recovery applications Expand climate-resilient housing investments and technical assistance Support disaster preparedness through resilience hubs, mutual aid networks, and inclusion of aging and disability providers and individuals with lived experience in local emergency planning Ensure emergency transportation plans explicitly include older adults and individuals with disabilities The housing challenges elevated through the Rural MPA Initiative align with research identifying rural housing stock as older, more likely to require repairs, and less accessible, while affordable rental options remain critically limited (Oberdorfer & Wiley, 2014). Rural communities also lack a full continuum of housing options that accommodate changing care needs, and rural older adults experience higher levels of unmet accessibility needs than urban counterparts (Anarde, 2019; Lee et al., 2025). Furthermore, the homeless population is aging with predisposing personal vulnerabilities (e.g., poverty and social isolation), structural factors (e.g., the lack of affordable housing), and the absence of a safety net (e.g., inadequate health care and social service networks) (Aron et al., 2001; Henderson et al., 2023). The recommendations in Table 2 emphasize a coordinated state response that scales proven tools (e.g., vouchers, home repair and modification programs, legal aid, and disaster navigation) while strengthening data systems to make rural older adult housing instability visible to policymakers. Collectively, these recommendations reflect a prevention-oriented approach that stabilizes housing before a temporary disaster becomes a long-term crisis and that strengthens housing plus services capacity where rural options are thinnest. Long waits for appointments, the compounding burden of transportation, and a pervasive struggle to navigate care define rural health care access—barriers exacerbated for those with disabilities or limited English proficiency. Critical structural gaps include workforce availability and care continuity, specialized geriatric and dementia expertise, integrated behavioral health care support, care coordination during transitions, transportation and digital infrastructure, and culturally responsive, trusted care. A cycle emerges where delayed or foregone care increases risks, caregiver strain, and preventable institutionalization. Table 3 summarizes the primary community-identified challenges within the health care domain and the corresponding state policy recommendations developed to address them (see also DeLange Martinez et al., 2025d). Health care access for rural older adults: from community-identified challenges to state policy recommendations. Expand rural training pipelines and residencies across primary care, behavioral health, emergency medicine, caregiving, and key specialties Support team-based, interdisciplinary care models through scope-of-practice alignment and reimbursement Provide rural recruitment and retention incentives (e.g., loan forgiveness, housing support, tax credits) Stabilize rural providers through targeted Medicaid rate adjustments and supplemental payments. Expand geriatric and dementia training in primary care and postgraduate education Fund continuing education on aging, disability, dementia, LGBTQ+ care, and culturally responsive care Support dementia-capable care models and caregiver education integrated into primary care Expand single points of entry for information, behavioral health support, counseling, and care coordination Strengthen hospital–community partnerships in discharge planning Improve interoperability and shared accountability across health and social care systems and fund electronic health record (EHR) upgrades in rural safety-net clinics Develop standardized discharge protocols for unhoused and high-risk older adults Fund flexible rural transportation models, including volunteer drivers and mileage reimbursement Stabilize rural Emergency Medical Services (EMS) through targeted state funding to close critical geographic service gaps Invest in broadband availability and affordability and digital literacy for older adults Support and reimburse telehealth navigators to assist patients Protect reimbursement for clinically appropriate virtual care Fund multilingual navigators and community health workers Partner with trusted rural and Tribal organizations, senior centers, community groups, and faith-based groups to deliver health education and support These experiences reflect a broader national paradox where the health care system faces growing complexity alongside declining capacity, a strain felt most acutely in rural regions (Jones & Dolsten, 2024). Access to timely and appropriate health care is a defining challenge for rural aging, shaped by a confluence of workforce shortages, geographic barriers, and fragmented systems. The policy directions in Table 3 move beyond isolated interventions, advocating for an integrated strategy that simultaneously builds the rural health care workforce, strengthens local care coordination, and ensures enabling supports like transportation and broadband are in place. Recent federal policy changes intensify the urgency of state-level rural aging policy action. The 2025 Budget Reconciliation Act (H.R. 1) imposes significant reductions to Medicaid—a primary funder of LTSS and health care for low-income older adults. These federal cuts are disproportionately straining state budgets and rural service infrastructures, where capacity is already thin. The recommendations in Tables 1–3 offer states practical strategies to scale and adapt existing state-administered programs - including recommendations that can be implemented even within a constrained fiscal environment. Importantly, proactive investment in these policies will ultimately yield long-term state savings by preventing costly hospitalizations and avoidable institutionalization. Long-term services and supports are threatened by H.R. 1’s restrictions on Medicaid financing, which make state-level cuts to optional HCBS more likely (ATI Advisory, 2025; Justice in Aging, 2025). Given that rural older adults already face shortages of professional caregivers and insufficient HCBS capacity, further reductions would exacerbate their reliance on unsupported informal networks. At the same time, chronic underfunding of Older Americans Act programs continues to weaken local aging networks responsible for critical outreach, navigation, and caregiver support (Phillips, 2025). Proactive state investment is essential to prevent further erosion of care capacity in these high need areas. Rural housing challenges are also intensified by recent federal shifts. Proposed reductions to rental assistance and changes to federal homelessness policy may disproportionately affect rural older adults, where affordable housing options and local capacity are already limited (Duke, 2025; Sequeira, 2025; U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development, 2025). In this context, state actions are vital to stabilize housing and preserve evidence-based navigation and prevention strategies. State-level actions around health care are urgent as H.R. 1 reduces projected federal Medicaid spending in rural areas alone by approximately $137 billion over a decade, with the majority of cuts occurring after 2030 (Kaiser Family Foundation, 2025). Although a temporary $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund was established for 2026–2030, its adequacy is uncertain and it sunsets just as rural aging populations surge and permanent cuts deepen (Kaiser Family Foundation, 2025). The health care recommendations provide a roadmap for states to use transitional federal funds to build resilient systems through developing the workforce, strengthening coordination, and stabilizing rural providers. The Rural MPA Initiative demonstrates a replicable pathway for translating rural lived experience into state action by pairing community listening with policy mapping and expert consultation, generating implementation-ready, cross-domain recommendations aligned with existing systems. ai_analysis.title_ko: 캘리포니아의 농어촌 고령화 정책 발전: 주거, 장기요양 서비스 및 지원, 의료 접근성에 관한 주 정부 정책 권고사항
ai_analysis.abstract_ko: 농어촌 지역은 도시 및 교외 지역보다 고령화가 더 빠르게 진행되고 있으며, 장애와 만성 질환의 부담이 커서 장기요양 서비스 및 지원(LTSS), 접근 가능한 주거, 의료 서비스에 대한 수요가 심화되고 있습니다. 이러한 수요는 지리적 고립, 인력 부족, 만성적 투자 부족, 저밀도 지역에 불리한 취약한 서비스 인프라와 같은 오랜 구조적 제약과 충돌합니다. 캘리포니아의 고령화 다부문 계획(MPA)은 현재 37개 주에서 채택하거나 검토 중인 모델로, 부문 간 조정을 위한 핵심 플랫폼을 제공합니다. 그러나 주 단위의 프레임워크를 농어촌 지역의 공평한 결과로 전환하려면 의도적인 참여와 정책 적응이 필요합니다. 2022년 스캔 재단(The SCAN Foundation)은 농어촌 MPA 이니셔티브를 시작하여 7개 카운티에 걸쳐 3개 농어촌 지역의 연합체를 지원했습니다. 집합적 영향 및 지역사회 참여 연구 원칙에 근거하여, 지역 연합체는 부문 간 자문위원회를 소집하고 계획 및 정책 수립 과정에서 역사적으로 소외되었던 주민들을 참여시켰습니다. 3년 동안 227명의 지역사회 구성원과 전문가가 초점 집단, 경청 세션, 인터뷰를 통해 정성적 의견을 제공했습니다. 이 의견은 2차 데이터와 결합되어 장벽을 파악하고 지역에 기반한 실행 계획을 개발하는 데 사용되었습니다. 2025년, 3개 지역에서 도출된 지역사회 식별 과제와 권고사항은 옹호 단체, 정부 기관, 농어촌 공급자를 포함한 82명의 주 및 지역 전문가와의 반복적인 협의를 거쳐 종합 및 정제되었습니다. 이 논문은 농어촌 노인, 돌봄 제공자, 서비스 제공자가 식별한 부문 간 과제를 설명하고, 주 및 지역 전문가와 공동 개발하고 다른 주에 적응시킨 실행 지향적 정책 권고사항을 제시합니다.
summary_3lines: 농어촌 지역의 급격한 고령화에 따른 장기요양, 주거, 의료 접근성 격차를 해소하기 위한 정책적 권고사항을 도출하고자 하였습니다.
지역사회 주민과 전문가들의 정성적 의견 수렴 및 2차 데이터 분석을 결합하여 지역 맞춤형 실행 계획을 수립하였습니다.
지리적 고립과 인력 부족 등 구조적 제약을 극복하기 위해 다부문 협력과 현장 중심의 정책 적응 체계를 구축해야 합니다.
ai_analysis.research_purpose: 본 연구는 농어촌 지역의 고령화로 인해 심화되는 장기요양 서비스, 주거, 의료 접근성의 격차를 진단하고, 이를 해결하기 위한 주 정부 차원의 실행 지향적 정책 권고사항을 개발하는 것을 목적으로 합니다. 특히 캘리포니아주의 고령화 다부문 계획(MPA) 사례를 바탕으로 지역사회의 목소리를 반영한 포괄적인 정책 모델을 제시하고자 하였습니다.
key_findings: 농어촌 지역은 도시 지역에 비해 장애 및 만성 질환 비율이 높으나 지리적 고립과 인력 부족으로 서비스 인프라가 취약함
지역사회 주민 및 전문가 227명의 정성적 피드백을 통해 주거, 장기요양, 의료 접근성에 대한 실질적인 장벽을 확인함
주 정부의 광범위한 정책 프레임워크를 현장 맞춤형으로 전환하기 위해 부문 간 협력 거버넌스와 지역 연합체의 역할이 필수적임
practical_applications: 국립공원 내 거주하는 고령 탐방객 및 공원 주변 지역 주민을 위한 맞춤형 편의 및 안전 인프라 확충
지리적으로 고립된 산간·도서 국립공원 주변 지역의 취약계층 지원을 위한 유관기관 간 협력 거버넌스 구축
현장 실무에서 고령 취약계층의 공원 이용 및 서비스 접근성 실태를 주기적으로 파악하는 모니터링 체계 도입
ai_analysis.korea_np_applicability_reason: 본 논문은 지역사회 노인 복지 및 보건의료 정책을 다루고 있어 국립공원 직접 관리 업무와는 거리가 있으나, 고령화가 진행되는 공원 주변 지역 주민 지원 및 탐방객 안전 관리 측면에서 간접적인 시사점을 제공합니다.
field_checklist: 공원 주변 고령 주민 및 탐방객 대상 서비스 이용 실태 조사 여부
지리적 취약 지역 내 안전 및 편의 인프라 현황 점검 여부
유관 지자체 및 보건 복지 부문과의 협력 체계 구축 여부
취약계층의 공원 탐방 시 애로사항 수렴 절차 마련 여부
현장 맞춤형 지원 정책 반영을 위한 정기적인 의견 청취 여부
cautions: 국립공원은 자연보호구역이므로 대규모 복지 인프라 설치 시 자연공원법에 저촉될 수 있음
보건·복지 서비스는 공원관리공단의 직접 소관 업무가 아니므로 지자체와의 긴밀한 협조가 전제되어야 함
recommended_followup_research: 국립공원 주변 농어촌 지역의 고령화가 탐방 및 지역 경제에 미치는 영향 분석
고령 탐방객 및 주변 주민을 위한 맞춤형 공원 서비스 모델 개발 연구
ai_recommended_topics: Long-term services and supports in rural areas

Patients in Real Clinic Settings Shoshanna Handel MPD,6 Elet Howe,2 Richard Zapata,1 Angela Burgess,3 Colleen Gillespie,7 Sondra Zabar MD,4 and David Stevens MD,5 1HEALTH CARE IMPROVEMENT, HEALTH AND HOSPITALS CORPORATION, NEW YORK, NY, USA, 2HEALTHCARE DELIVERY IMPROVEMENT, NEW YORK CITY HEALTH & HOSPITALS CORPORATION, NEW YORK, NY, USA, 3MEDICINE, NEW YORK UNIVERSITY, NEW YORK, NY, USA and 4MEDICINE, NEW YORK UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF MEDICINE, NEW YORK, NY, USA, 5OFFICE OF HEALTHCARE IMPROVEMENT, NYC HEALTH & HOSPITALS CORPORATION, NEW YORK, NY, USA, 6HEALTHCARE IMPROVEMENT, NYC HEALTH AND HOSPITALS CORPORATION, NEW YORK, NY, USA, and 7MEDICINE, NYU SCHOOL OF MEDICINE, NEW YORK, NY, USA. 4th Place – 1291 Program Improvement Through Standardized Simulation Testing Joanne Weinschreider RN, MS,1 1NURSING, ST JOHN FISHER COLLEGE, ROCHESTER, NY, USA. 44 Achieving Curriculum Standardization in a Distributed Human Patient Simulator Network Douglas Howard MS, RN,1 1MEDICAL MODERNIZATION, UNITED STATES AIR FORCE, RANDOLPH AFB, TX, USA Introduction/Background: Standardization of curriculum using simulation has been shown to improve skill acquisition, retention and reduce complications in the performance of the simulator-trained skill in practice.1,2 The Air Force Medical Service (AFMS) has over 80 sites around the globe in a distributed human patient simulator program which uses multiple types and brands of medical training simulators. Larger facilities have full time staff trained to operate equipment. Smaller facilities use active duty members on a part time basis that may not have proper training to function as effective operators and use simulators intermittently for training. Frequent rotation of active duty members requires re-training locally, for a fee, through the vendor or by traveling to another location, both of which are prohibitively expensive in a large system. Due to these gaps, there is currently a need for a distributed basic simulation operator’s course for each type of simulator. The variation and number of different computer programs required to operate the simulators further complicates the problem. Although standardized requirements exist in the Readiness Skills Verification Program (RSVP), there is no method for measuring compliance with these RSVPs across multiple sites using simulation. Description: A series of RSVP scenarios were developed through the Air Force Medical Modeling and Simulation Training (AFMMAST) office to address the lack of standardized curricula. AFMMAST distributes these scenarios in a template format which includes standardized performance metrics for both task and interprofessional team performance. Each scenario is programmed into the major simulator types used at the small sites using critical objectives as branch points. Coupled with this program is a detailed scenario description including scripts, debriefing questions, performance checklists and continuing medical education credits. Development of each scenario is based upon current practice literature, clinical guidelines and lessons learned from the deployed units. The scenarios end in one of 4 possible scores depending on how well the team addresses the critical objectives. Although primarily designed for use at the smaller sites without full time operators, these scenarios can also be used at the larger sites. Scenarios are developed as an entire patient encounter encompassing various clinical locations (e.g. ED, ICU, Air Evacuation, etc.), but are broken into smaller modules so that they can be successfully executed at the smaller sites in shorter time slots. This method of programming performance measures allows for the facilitator to pinpoint where participants deviated from the ‘ideal state’ and the simulator records the observed performance for use in the debriefing. Scenarios programmed in this manner using a standardized curriculum minimize variation due to operator and facilitator experience or facility size. In order to facilitate use of these standard scenarios, a web-based simulation operator training program is being developed, which is self-paced with job aids and will be evaluated by the ability of the novice operator to successfully upload and run a standard scenario. Conclusion: This level of standardization is possible, but it requires significant familiarity with the equipment and various methods of programming the simulators. Challenges include simulators of various ages and brands using multiple scenario development approaches in the AFMS system. Additionally, sustainment of these various models of simulation equipment and maintaining computer programs with the latest updates continue to be an issue. We believe that this new method of standardizing a simulation operator training course and providing “plug and play” scenarios for the end user will allow for higher confidence in the inexperienced operators and encourage more frequent use of simulation at the smaller facilities. Finally, attaching performance metrics to the standardized scenario template and programming will instill higher confidence in leadership that their Airmen are prepared to complete their wartime missions. References: 1. Simulation-based training is superior to problem-based learning for the acquisition of critical assessment and management skills. Steadman R, Coates W, Huang Y, Matevosian R, Larmon B, McCullough L, Ariel D. Crit Care Med 2006 Vol. 34, No.1 pp 151–57. PubMed PMID:16374169. 2.
